transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: A new study has found that drinking tea may be linked to a lower risk of heart disease and stroke, according to researchers at the University of Cambridge. The study followed over 100,000 people for more than 10 years and found that people who drank at least three cups of tea per day had a 20 percent lower risk of heart disease and a 24 percent lower risk of stroke compared to people who didn't drink tea. Both black tea and green tea showed benefits, though green tea had slightly stronger effects. Researchers say tea contains antioxidants called flavonoids, which are known to reduce inflammation and improve blood vessel function. They also note that the way tea is prepared matters—adding milk, sugar, or cream can cancel out some of the health benefits. The study adds to growing evidence that tea, when consumed in moderation without too much added sugar, can be part of a healthy diet. However, researchers caution that tea is not a magic bullet, and overall diet and lifestyle are still the most important factors for heart health.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: The city of Portland, Oregon has become one of the first cities in the United States to ban single-use plastic straws, utensils, and stirrers in restaurants and food service businesses, as part of the city's efforts to reduce plastic waste and protect the environment. The ban applies to all restaurants, cafes, food trucks, and other food establishments, which can only provide single-use plastic items if a customer specifically requests them. Businesses are encouraged to use paper, compostable, or reusable alternatives instead. The city says that single-use plastics are a major source of pollution, especially in rivers and oceans, where they harm wildlife and take hundreds of years to decompose. Portland has long been a leader in environmental policies, and this ban is part of a broader effort to reduce waste and move toward a zero-waste economy. While some businesses have expressed concerns about the cost of switching to alternatives, the city says the long-term environmental benefits far outweigh the short-term costs. The city also plans to expand the ban to other single-use plastic items in the coming years.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Scientists at the University of California, Berkeley have developed a new type of solar panel that can generate electricity from rain as well as sunlight, opening up new possibilities for solar power in rainy and cloudy regions. The panels use a special transparent coating that generates electricity when raindrops hit it, using the kinetic energy of the falling rain. While the amount of electricity generated from rain is much less than from sunlight, it could help solar panels continue to produce power on cloudy and rainy days when traditional solar panels are less effective. Researchers say this technology could be especially useful in places with lots of rain, like the Pacific Northwest of the United States or parts of Northern Europe, where solar power hasn't been as practical because of the cloudy weather. The technology is still in the early stages of development, and the current prototypes are not very efficient, but researchers are working to improve the design and increase the amount of electricity that can be generated from rain. They hope the technology could be commercially available within the next decade.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Sarah): Hey Jake, I heard you're learning how to cook. How's that going?
Man (Jake): It's going... okay, I guess. I'm still really bad at it, but I'm trying.
Woman: Why did you decide to learn to cook? I remember you used to eat takeout every night.

Man: Yeah, well, my doctor said my cholesterol is too high and I need to eat healthier. Takeout is so greasy and salty, and I'm gaining weight. So I figured if I cook at home, I can control what goes into my food and make it healthier.
Woman: That's a great reason! Cooking at home is definitely healthier than eating out all the time. What have you been making?
Man: Oh, just simple stuff. I tried making pasta last week, and it turned out okay. And I made scrambled eggs for breakfast this morning—they were a little burnt, but edible.
Woman: Ha, that's a start! Everyone burns eggs when they're first learning. Do you have the right equipment?
Man: I don't think so. My knives are really dull, and I only have one frying pan. And my cutting board is tiny. I feel like I'm working in a toy kitchen.
Woman: Yeah, having good equipment makes a big difference. You don't need anything fancy, but a good sharp knife and a decent pan go a long way. Do you have any cookbooks or anything?
Man: No, I've just been watching videos online and following recipes I find on the internet. But it's hard because I don't always know what the terms mean. Like, what's "sauté" anyway?
Woman: Ha, sauté is just cooking something quickly in a little oil or butter over medium-high heat. It's not that complicated. You'll pick up the terms as you go.
Man: I hope so. Another problem is that I'm cooking for just one person, so I end up buying all these ingredients and then they go bad before I can use them. It feels like such a waste.

Woman: Oh, I know what you mean. Cooking for one is tricky. You could try making bigger batches and eating leftovers for a few days. Or you could freeze portions for later. That way you don't waste food and you always have something ready to eat.
Man: That's a good idea. I never thought about freezing things. What else do you think I should know?

Woman: Hmm... don't be afraid to make mistakes. Everyone burns things or messes up recipes when they're learning. The important thing is to keep trying and have fun with it. And start simple—don't try to make some complicated French dish on your first day. Master the basics first.
Man: Yeah, that makes sense. Hey, would you maybe want to cook together sometime? You're a really good cook, and I could learn a lot from you.

Woman: Sure! That sounds like fun. How about this weekend? We can make something simple but delicious, like stir-fry or roasted chicken and vegetables. I'll bring some of my extra tools, and we can cook together.
Man: That would be awesome! Thanks so much, Sarah. I really appreciate it.
Woman: No problem! Cooking is more fun with friends anyway. And who knows—maybe you'll be a great cook someday.
Man: I doubt it, but I'll try.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Ethan): Hey Ava, how's your Etsy shop going? I saw you posted some new jewelry the other day—it looks really nice.

Woman (Ava): Thanks! Yeah, I've been making a lot of new pieces lately. But honestly, the shop isn't doing as well as I hoped. I'm not making very many sales, and I'm starting to wonder if it's worth it.
Man: Oh, that's too bad. What do you think the problem is?
Woman: I'm not sure. I think my stuff is good, but no one seems to be finding my shop. It's like my listings are invisible or something. I don't know how to get people to look at my stuff.

Man: Yeah, getting noticed is the hardest part, especially when you're just starting out. There are so many shops on Etsy, it's hard to stand out. Have you tried using social media to promote your work?
Woman: A little bit. I have an Instagram account, but I only have like 50 followers, and most of them are my friends. I don't know how to get more people to see it.

Man: Social media takes time to build up, but it can be really effective if you do it right. You should post more—like every day if you can. And post different kinds of things: photos of your jewelry, behind-the-scenes shots of you making it, videos of the process... people love seeing how things are made.
Woman: Really? I thought people just wanted to see the finished product.
Man: No, the story behind the product is just as important. People want to connect with the maker and know who's making their jewelry and how. It makes the product more meaningful.
Woman: That's a good point. What else?

Man: You should use hashtags—specific ones, not just #jewelry or #handmade, which are too broad. Use more specific hashtags like #handmadeearrings or #etsyjewelry or #artisanjewelry. And engage with other people's posts too—comment on other makers' posts, join jewelry-making communities... that helps get your name out there.
Woman: Hmm, okay. I'll try that. What about pricing? I'm worried my prices are too high, but I also don't want to sell myself short. It takes me hours to make each piece.

Man: Pricing is tricky. A lot of new makers underprice their work because they don't value their time. You have to remember that you're not just selling materials—you're selling your time, your skill, and your creativity. If your prices are too low, people might actually think your work is lower quality.
Woman: Really? I thought lower prices would mean more sales.

Man: Sometimes, but not always. People associate price with quality. If something is too cheap, they wonder what's wrong with it. You want to price your work fairly—cover your materials, pay yourself for your time, and make a profit. That's how you build a sustainable business.
Woman: That makes sense. I think I might be undercharging. What else can I do to get more sales?

Man: You could try doing craft fairs or local markets. Selling in person is great because people can see and touch your jewelry, and they get to meet you. It's also a good way to get feedback and build a local customer base.
Woman: I've thought about that, but I'm kind of nervous about talking to people.
Man: Oh, it's scary at first, but you get used to it. And it's really rewarding when someone buys something you made and tells you how much they love it. You should try it!
Woman: Maybe I will. Thanks for all the advice, Ethan. You've given me a lot to think about.
Man: No problem! Your jewelry is really nice, you just need to get it in front of the right people. Keep at it, and I'm sure you'll be successful.
Woman: I hope you're right.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The history of writing is one of the most important inventions in human history, allowing us to record information, communicate across distances, and pass knowledge down from generation to generation. Before writing was invented, information could only be passed down orally, which meant it could be forgotten or changed over time. Writing changed all that, making it possible to preserve ideas, laws, stories, and knowledge permanently.

The earliest known writing systems developed independently in several different parts of the world around the same time. The oldest known writing system is cuneiform, which was developed in Mesopotamia (in present-day Iraq) around 3500 BC. Cuneiform was written by pressing a reed stylus into soft clay tablets, creating wedge-shaped marks. It was used for thousands of years and was adapted to write several different languages.

Around the same time, writing also developed in Egypt. Egyptian hieroglyphs are perhaps the most famous ancient writing system, with their picture-like symbols. Hieroglyphs were used for religious and formal purposes, and they were carved into stone and painted on walls. The Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799, was the key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs, as it had the same text written in hieroglyphs, Demotic (another Egyptian script), and ancient Greek.

Writing also developed independently in China. Chinese writing is one of the oldest writing systems still in use today, with a history going back over 3,000 years. Unlike most other writing systems, Chinese is logographic—each character represents a word or idea rather than a sound. There are thousands of Chinese characters, and learning to read and write Chinese takes many years.

Another important writing system developed in Mesoamerica, where the Maya and other civilizations had their own hieroglyphic writing systems. Maya script was only fully deciphered in the late 20th century, and it has given us a much better understanding of Maya history and culture.

Over time, writing systems evolved from pictures and symbols to more abstract representations of sounds. The alphabet, where each symbol represents a single sound, was a major innovation. The first alphabet was developed by the Phoenicians around 1000 BC, and it became the basis for many modern alphabets, including Greek, Latin, and eventually English.

Today, writing is everywhere—from books and newspapers to emails and text messages. It's hard to imagine a world without writing. It's one of the inventions that made civilization possible, and it continues to shape how we communicate, learn, and think.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: The placebo effect is a fascinating phenomenon in medicine where a person's belief in a treatment can cause real improvements in their condition, even if the treatment itself has no actual medical value. The word "placebo" comes from Latin and means "I shall please." Placebos are usually sugar pills or injections with no active ingredients, but they can also be fake surgeries or other treatments that don't actually do anything medically.

The placebo effect has been documented in thousands of medical studies. In many clinical trials, people who receive a placebo instead of real medicine still show improvements in their symptoms. This is why new drugs have to be tested against placebos—to make sure that the drug actually works better than just the belief that it works.

But how does the placebo effect actually work? How can believing that you're getting treatment make you actually feel better? Scientists are still learning about all the mechanisms involved, but there are several explanations.

One explanation is that the placebo effect works through the power of expectation. If you believe a treatment will make you better, your brain might actually trigger changes in your body that make you feel better. For example, expecting pain relief can cause your brain to release endorphins, which are natural painkillers. Studies have shown that placebos can actually reduce pain in many people, and this effect can be blocked by drugs that stop endorphins from working.

Another explanation is that the ritual of receiving treatment—going to the doctor, taking a pill, being cared for—reduces stress and anxiety, and stress can make many health conditions worse. When you feel cared for and supported, your body's stress response decreases, which can help your immune system work better and help you heal faster.

The placebo effect is not just "in your head"—it has real physical effects on the body. Studies have shown that placebos can affect heart rate, blood pressure, brain activity, and even immune function. It's a real biological effect, not just imagination.

Interestingly, the placebo effect works even when people know they're taking a placebo. Studies have found that "open-label placebos"—placebos that people know are placebos—can still be effective for conditions like pain, depression, and irritable bowel syndrome. This suggests that the placebo effect is more complex than just fooling people.

There's also the opposite of the placebo effect, called the nocebo effect. This is when believing a treatment will harm you actually causes negative side effects. For example, if people are told a drug might cause headaches, some people will get headaches even if they're just taking a sugar pill.

The placebo effect shows how powerful the mind-body connection is. It's a reminder that healing isn't just about drugs and surgery—our beliefs, expectations, and emotions also play an important role in our health.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Urbanization—the process of people moving from rural areas to cities and the growth of cities—is one of the most important trends of the modern world. Today, more than half of the world's population lives in cities, and that number is expected to grow to nearly 70 percent by 2050. This rapid urbanization is changing how we live, work, and interact with each other, and it presents both enormous challenges and opportunities.

Cities have always been centers of culture, commerce, and innovation. Throughout history, cities have been where new ideas are born, where art and science flourish, and where people from different backgrounds come together. Cities are also engines of economic growth—they generate most of the world's GDP and create most of the world's jobs. The concentration of people, businesses, and resources in cities creates opportunities that just don't exist in rural areas.

However, rapid urbanization also brings many challenges. One of the biggest challenges is housing. As more and more people move to cities, housing becomes scarce and expensive. In many cities around the world, especially in developing countries, millions of people live in slums and informal settlements with no access to clean water, sanitation, or basic services. These informal settlements are often overcrowded, unsafe, and unhealthy.

Traffic congestion is another major problem in cities. As cities grow and more people own cars, roads become clogged with traffic, leading to long commute times, air pollution, and wasted time and money. Many cities are trying to address this by investing in public transportation, building bike lanes, and creating walkable neighborhoods, but it's a constant challenge.

Air pollution is another serious issue in many cities. Cars, factories, and power plants release pollutants into the air, which can cause respiratory problems, heart disease, and other health issues. Air pollution is especially bad in fast-growing cities in developing countries, where environmental regulations are often weaker.

Despite these challenges, cities also have great potential to be sustainable and livable. Dense cities can actually be more environmentally friendly per person than rural areas because people drive less, share resources more efficiently, and public transportation is more practical. Cities can also invest in renewable energy, green buildings, parks and green spaces, and sustainable water and waste management systems.

The key to successful urbanization is good planning. Cities that plan ahead, invest in infrastructure and public services, and prioritize the needs of all their residents—especially low-income and marginalized communities—can be great places to live. But cities that grow without planning can face serious problems that are hard to fix later.

As more and more people move to cities in the coming decades, the challenge of building sustainable, livable, and inclusive cities will become one of the most important issues of the 21st century. How we design and build our cities will shape not just how we live, but also the future of the planet.
